entry: Chinese emperor of the [[Ming dynasty]] (r. 1521–1567). He succeeded his cousin, the Zhengde Emperor, who died without an heir. His unexpected accession led to the Great Rites Controversy, a three-year dispute with officials over how to legalize it, which ended with his main opponents banished or executed. In 1542 he moved to the West Park, west of the [[Forbidden City]], where he built palaces and Taoist temples and pursued immortality. His elixirs contained harmful substances such as arsenic, lead and [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], which may have shortened his life. The emperor refused Mongol demands for restored free trade and attempted to close the borders with fortifications, including the [[Great Wall of China]]. Altan Khan's raids reached the outskirts of [[Beijing]] in 1550. Wokou piracy escalated through the 1540s and peaked in the 1550s. Despite trade restrictions and the deadly [[1556 Shaanxi earthquake]], the economy continued to grow in agriculture, industry and trade.

Chinese revolutionary, actress and political figure; fourth wife of [[Mao Zedong]]. She grew up with an abusive father, joined the [[Chinese Communist Party]] (CCP) in 1933 and pursued an acting career in [[Shanghai]] before going to Yan'an, where she married Mao in 1938. After 1949 she wielded considerable influence over the arts and engaged in party power struggles, orchestrating campaigns against the film *The Life of Wu Xun* and the Peking opera *Hai Rui Dismissed from Office*. A Politburo member, she played a major role in the [[Cultural Revolution]] and led the Gang of Four, reaching the height of her power in the late 1960s. After Mao's death she was arrested and expelled from the party. Sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve in a televised trial, she had her sentence commuted to [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]], and she died by [[Suicide|suicide]] in prison.

Chinese politician; fourth paramount leader of China (1989–2002). He became general secretary of the [[Chinese Communist Party]] (CCP) as a compromise candidate after the [[1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre]], replacing Zhao Ziyang, who had been ousted for supporting the student movement. He was president from 1993 to 2003 and chaired the Central Military Commission from 1989 to 2004. In 1992 he introduced the term socialist market economy, which accelerated [[Reform and opening up|reform and opening up]]. His administration privatized many state-owned enterprises, and China joined the [[World Trade Organization]] in 2001. Under him Hong Kong returned from the United Kingdom in 1997 and Macau from Portugal in 1999. His Three Represents doctrine legitimized the entry of private business owners into the party. In 1999 he began a crackdown on [[Falun Gong]]. He gave up his posts to [[Hu Jintao]] between 2002 and 2005, although his faction continued to influence affairs.

Coastal province in East China, with its capital at [[Nanjing]]. It is the third smallest province but the fourth most populous, with 84.75 million people, and the most densely populated of China's 22 provinces. Jiangsu has the highest GDP per capita and the second-largest GDP of any province, after [[Guangdong]]. It has been a commercial center since the Sui and Tang dynasties, partly because of the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]]. Its coastline of over 1,000 kilometers (620 mi) lies on the [[Yellow Sea]], and the [[Yangtze]] flows through the south of the province. Jiangsu became the first province in China to reach the $20,000 mark in GDP per capita, in 2021, and it has been China's largest recipient of foreign direct investment since 2006. As of 2022 it hosted 168 institutions of higher education, the most of any province.

Tiling puzzle made of interlocking, often irregularly shaped pieces that must be assembled to match a picture. In the 18th century puzzles were made by painting a picture on wood and cutting it apart; the name derives from the saws used to cut them. John Spilsbury, a [[London]] cartographer and engraver, is credited with commercializing the puzzle around 1760, using world [[Map|maps]] cut along national borders so that students could reassemble them. Cardboard pieces appeared in the late 1800s. Puzzles became a craze among American adults from 1907 to 1910 and soared in popularity during the [[Great Depression]]. Typical subjects include nature scenes, buildings and [[Castle|castles]], although any picture can be used. Competitive puzzling has grown in popularity in the 21st century, with annual World Jigsaw Puzzle Championships held from 2019.

British character actor. He won an Academy Award for his supporting role as John Bayley in *Iris* (2001). His television work includes the [[BBC]] sitcom Only Fools and Horses and [[Game of Thrones]], and he played Horace Slughorn in the [[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]] films. He also won a BAFTA Award for playing Lord Longford in the television film *Longford* (2006).

American professional football player and actor. Playing fullback for the Cleveland Browns of the [[National Football League]] from 1957 to 1965, he led the league in rushing yards in eight of his nine seasons and was AP NFL Most Valuable Player three times. He retired at the peak of his career to act, obtaining 53 acting credits, including *100 Rifles* (1969). He spoke out on racial issues during the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]], founded the Black Economic Union and facilitated a truce between rival street gangs in [[Los Angeles]].

Canadian-American actor and comedian. Known for energetic slapstick, he became a film star with *Ace Ventura: Pet Detective* and *The Mask* (both 1994). He was the first comic actor to receive an upfront $20 million salary for films, beginning with *The Cable Guy* (1996). He won Golden Globe Awards for *The Truman Show* (1998) and for playing [[Andy Kaufman]] in *Man on the Moon* (1999). Later films include *Yes Man* (2008).

American voice actor and podcaster. Since the 1980s he has appeared in more than 600 titles. He has been the official voice of Winnie the Pooh since 1988 and of Tigger since 1989 for [[The Walt Disney Company]], and he has voiced the Tasmanian Devil since 1991 for Warner Bros. After moving to [[New Orleans]] he designed Mardi Gras floats and played drums in the rock band Fusion.

American puppeteer and filmmaker; creator of the Muppets. He co-founded Muppets, Inc. (now The Jim Henson Company) with his future wife, Jane Nebel, in 1958. In 1969 he joined [[Sesame Street]], where he helped develop its Muppet characters, and he developed Kermit the Frog and Rowlf the Dog. He produced The Muppet Show (1976–1981) and created Fraggle Rock (1983–1987). He directed the films *The Dark Crystal* (1982) and *Labyrinth* (1986). He revolutionized the way [[Puppetry|puppetry]] is captured and presented on video and won two Emmy Awards. He was posthumously awarded a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1991.

American cult leader; founder of the Peoples Temple, a [[New religious movement]]. Jones moved the group to California and in 1974 ordered construction of the [[Jonestown]] commune in Guyana. After U.S. Congressman Leo Ryan investigated reports of abuse, gunmen from Jonestown killed Ryan and four others at an airstrip. Jones then directed a mass murder–suicide in which over 900 people died, approximately 396 of them children, most by drinking Flavor Aid laced with [[Cyanide|cyanide]]. Most of his followers, and later victims, were African American.

American singer-songwriter and poet; lead vocalist of [[The Doors]]. Morrison co-founded the band with Ray Manzarek in 1965 in Venice, California. Its number-one US hit, "Light My Fire", came from the self-titled debut album. His stage performances were provocative, including an arrest on stage in New Haven and a controversial Miami concert in 1969. He developed an alcohol dependency. He died in [[Paris]], and since no autopsy was performed, the cause of death remains disputed. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1993.

American multisport athlete and citizen of the Sac and Fox Nation. Thorpe won the pentathlon and decathlon at the 1912 Summer Olympics, becoming the first Native American to win a gold medal for the United States. His medals were stripped after it was found that he had been paid for two seasons of semi-professional baseball before the Games, violating amateurism rules. The International Olympic Committee later restored replica medals and, in 2022, recognized him as sole champion of both events. He played six seasons in [[Major League Baseball]] with the New York Giants and helped the Canton Bulldogs win three professional football championships. His career ended as the [[Great Depression]] began, and he struggled in poverty afterward. The Associated Press named him the greatest athlete of the first 50 years of the 20th century.

American guitarist and singer-songwriter. After enlisting in the US Army in 1961, Hendrix played backing roles for the Isley Brothers and [[Little Richard]] before moving to England in 1966, where he formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience. The group had three UK top-ten hits, including "Purple Haze," and his fame in the US grew after the Monterey Pop Festival. His album *Electric Ladyland* (1968) was his only number-one album on the US Billboard 200. He headlined the [[Woodstock|Woodstock]] Festival in 1969 and was instrumental in popularizing feedback as a musical sound. He used fuzz, Octavia and wah-wah effects, and he died in London from [[Barbiturate|barbiturate]]-related [[Asphyxia|asphyxia]]. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1992.

American politician and humanitarian; 39th [[President of the United States|president of the United States]] (1977–1981). A Democrat, he narrowly defeated incumbent [[Gerald Ford]] in 1976. He negotiated the Camp David Accords and the Panama Canal Treaties and established diplomatic relations with China. His term was marked by the [[Iranian Revolution]] and the [[Iran hostage crisis]]. He lost reelection to [[Ronald Reagan]] in a landslide. Afterward he founded the Carter Center to promote human rights and won the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize.

American comedian and television host. He joined the cast of [[Saturday Night Live]] in 1998 and co-hosted its Weekend Update segment before leaving in 2004 for film roles, including *Taxi* (2004). He hosted Late Night with Jimmy Fallon on [[NBC]] from 2009 to 2014, then became the sixth permanent host of The Tonight Show, succeeding [[Jay Leno]]. He has won four Primetime Emmy Awards and a Grammy Award.

American labor union leader; general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters from 1957 to 1971. He secured the first national agreement for teamsters' rates, in 1964, and the union grew to over 2.3 million members under his leadership. He had ties to [[Organized crime]] and was convicted in 1964 of jury tampering, attempted bribery and conspiracy. Imprisoned in 1967 with a 13-year sentence, he was released in 1971 after [[Richard Nixon]] commuted it, on condition that he stay out of union activities until 1980. He disappeared in 1975 under mysterious circumstances and is thought to have been murdered by the Mafia.

American television host and comedian. He is the host and executive producer of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, which has aired on ABC since 2003. Before that he co-hosted Comedy Central's The Man Show. He has hosted the [[Academy Awards]] four times, and in 2018 [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world. At 23 seasons, his tenure hosting a late-night comedy-variety show is second only to [[Johnny Carson]]. In 2025 ABC suspended the show for a week after Kimmel commented on the assassination of Charlie Kirk in his monologue.

English guitarist and producer; founder of [[Led Zeppelin]]. Page began as a session musician in London and was a member of the Yardbirds from 1966 to 1968. He then formed Led Zeppelin, which was active until 1980, when drummer John Bonham died. Afterward he played with other groups, including Coverdale–Page and Page and Plant. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him No. 3 on its 2015 list of the "100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time." He has been inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] twice, and he has a long interest in the occult, especially the writings of [[Aleister Crowley]].

English disc jockey and television presenter. He hosted the [[BBC]] shows Top of the Pops and Jim'll Fix It, and he raised an estimated £40 million for charities, including hospitals. He was knighted in 1990. After his death, hundreds of allegations of sexual abuse were investigated, and police concluded that he had been a predatory sex offender, possibly one of the UK's most prolific. Some honours were posthumously revoked. Investigations at 28 NHS hospitals concluded that he had sexually assaulted staff and patients.

Chinese [[Wuxia|wuxia]] novelist; pen name of Louis Cha Leung-yung. Cha worked as a journalist and translator for the Shanghai newspaper *Ta Kung Pao* before moving to Hong Kong in 1948. He co-founded the Hong Kong newspaper *Ming Pao* and authored 15 novels between 1955 and 1972. Over 100 million copies have sold worldwide, excluding pirated editions, and his novels have been adapted into TV dramas, films and video games. They are esteemed for their literary quality and appeal to scholarly and popular audiences. Cha later earned a doctorate in Asian Studies from the [[University of Cambridge]].

Jurchen-led imperial dynasty of China, ruled by the Wanyan clan (1115–1234). The dynasty emerged from Wanyan Aguda's rebellion against the [[Liao dynasty]], and its official name, Great Jin, means "gold." After conquering Liao territory, the Jin waged a century-long campaign against the [[Song dynasty]] in southern China. Its emperors adopted Han customs, fortified the Great Wall against the rising [[Mongol Empire]], and oversaw a revival of [[Confucianism]]. In 1211 the Mongols, led by [[Genghis Khan]], invaded and won several victories. Over 23 years the Jin faced defeats, revolts, defections and coups, and the Mongols finally conquered them in 1234.

Imperial dynasty of China (266–420), founded by Sima Yan. It succeeded the Cao Wei kingdom and in 280 conquered Eastern Wu, ending the [[Three Kingdoms]] period and reuniting China proper for the first time since the [[Han dynasty]] ended. Civil wars from 291 to 306, the War of the Eight Princes, weakened the state. Non-Han rebellions followed, ushering in the [[Sixteen Kingdoms]] era. The Han-Zhao state sacked [[Luoyang]] in 311 and executed Emperor Min in 318, ending the Western Jin. Sima Rui then re-established the dynasty at Jiankang, modern [[Nanjing]]. The Eastern Jin remained in near-constant conflict with northern states until General Liu Yu usurped it in 420.

City (pop. 9.2 million), capital of [[Shandong]] province in eastern China. Its name means "south of the Ji," referring to the Ji River, which flowed north of the city until the [[Yellow River]] took over its bed in 1852. The area has been inhabited for more than 4000 years, including during the [[Neolithic]] Longshan culture. Jinan is called the "City of Springs" for its 72 artesian springs. It has held sub-provincial administrative status since 1994 and is a major national administrative, economic and transportation hub. The city is home to several universities, including Shandong University, and ranked 27th in the world for scientific research in the Nature Index 2025 Science Cities.

Supernatural beings in [[Islam]], pre-Islamic Arabian religion and Arabic folklore. Like humans, jinn are accountable for their deeds and can be believers or unbelievers. They are naturally invisible and can shapeshift, usually appearing as [[Snake|snakes]], [[Scorpion|scorpions]], [[Lizard|lizards]] or humans. They rarely meddle in human affairs, but if harmed they may retaliate, sometimes by possessing the assailant, which requires exorcism. The [[Quran]] condemns the pre-Islamic practice of seeking protection from them. Folk practices, such as amulets against their assaults, have met increasing disapproval because of their association with idolatry. The word derives from a Semitic root meaning "to hide" or "to adapt."
